description: Solo team building FireSight, a web app that harmonizes NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS active-fire hotspots into one consistent burning-activity calendar from 2000 to today. Pick any area by drawing it, searching or entering coordinates, see which months and years burned most, compare this month against the historical median, and download the hotspots and analytics as CSV. Built for fire managers, responders and land managers.
summary:
FireSight is a web app that turns 25 years of NASA FIRMS active-fire hotspots into one consistent burning-activity calendar for any area you choose.

MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012) see the same fires very differently: VIIRS reports about three times as many hotspots, so a raw record jumps when VIIRS arrives. FireSight harmonizes the two. It applies the same quality rules to both sensors, fills satellite outages from their sister satellites, and cross-calibrates MODIS to the VIIRS scale on days when all three satellites observed, with separate day and night factors, 90% uncertainty intervals and cross-validated error. In Argentina the held-out monthly error falls from 69% to 6.8%, so the sensor of origin no longer matters.

Users draw an area, search a region or enter coordinates, then see which months and years burned most, how this month compares with the historical median, when the fire season runs, the long-term trend, and every hotspot on a map. Everything downloads as CSV, JSON, PNG or a printed report.

Fire managers and responders get a consistent baseline to recognise unusual activity early and plan for critical periods.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

FireSight answers the questions a fire manager asks about an area:

  • When does this area burn? Fire season, peak month and the monthly climatology.
  • Which months and years burned most? A years-by-months burning calendar with accessible colour ramps, annual totals and a significance-tested trend.
  • Is now unusual? This month so far and the last 7 days, each compared with the same days in every past year: the normal range, the median, the rank, and a status from Below normal to Record.
  • What is burning now? A map of every hotspot, coloured by fire radiative power, age or sensor, with the time and coordinates of each.
  • How does this fire compare? Any period against the same calendar window in every year, plus a weekly and daily record of every year since 2000.
  • Can I take it with me? CSV of every hotspot with its harmonized weight, monthly, daily, annual, climatology and calibration tables, a JSON report, PNG and SVG charts, a printable report and shareable links.

Areas can be drawn on the map (rectangle, polygon, circle), picked from provinces and countries, entered as latitude and longitude, or uploaded as GeoJSON.

HOW THE HARMONIZATION WORKS

  1. Same quality rules for both sensors: MODIS confidence 30 or more and VIIRS nominal or high, vegetation fires only, and known static sources (gas flares, industry, volcanoes) removed by location in every year.
  2. A common counting unit: detections, or unique 1 km "fire cell-days", which collapse several VIIRS pixels inside one MODIS-sized footprint.
  3. Continuity within each sensor family: days when Terra or Aqua was missing are scaled from the days both flew; S-NPP outages are filled from NOAA-20, so the growing satellite constellation does not inflate recent years. Outages, partial days and S-NPP's end in November 2026 are detected from the data itself, so a missing day never reads as a day without fires.
  4. Cross-calibration on the overlap: on days all three satellites observed (2012–2019), the VIIRS/MODIS ratio is estimated by month and separately for day and night (VIIRS gains about 7x at night against 2.7x by day in central Argentina). Small areas borrow strength from a regional prior. A year-block bootstrap gives 90% intervals, and leave-one-year-out cross-validation chooses the model and reports its error.
  5. The harmonized record: observed VIIRS wherever it exists and calibrated MODIS before 2012, on the VIIRS scale (or the reverse, on the MODIS scale).

DOES IT WORK?

  • Held-out monthly error, raw counts to harmonized: Argentina 69% to 6.8% (R² 0.991), United States 71% to 6.6%, Paraguay 68% to 6.5%.
  • Trends agree in sign and size on the VIIRS and MODIS scales, so they are not an artifact of the harmonization.
  • 107 automated tests plant known sensor differences and outages and check the engine recovers them. A separate Python program, written from the method description, recomputes the record from the raw FIRMS archive files and matched the app on all six test cases through 2025; this year's days, fetched through the FIRMS API, are not yet in its inputs.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Emergency managers get one consistent 25-year baseline instead of two incompatible records, so they can see whether this month or this week is unusual for their area, anticipate the critical part of the season, and back their decisions with numbers they can download and share. The app is honest about uncertainty: calibrated years carry intervals, days without satellite data are shown as no data rather than zero fires, and every statistic states its baseline.

CREATIVITY AND DESIGN CHOICES

The signature view rates current activity on a five-class scale styled like the fire-danger ratings crews already read. Day and night calibration, fire cell-days and data-driven outage detection go beyond a single conversion factor. The interface was tested from the point of view of a fire officer on desktop and phone, in light and dark themes.

COVERAGE

The current build covers Argentina, Chile, Uruguay, Paraguay, Portugal, Greece and the United States: about 27.5 million FIRMS detections from November 2000 to November 2026, including near-real-time data.

TOOLS

TypeScript, Next.js 16, React 19, MapLibre GL, D3, Tailwind CSS and Vitest for the app; Python with SciPy, pymannkendall and pyproj for the independent audit.

USE OF AI

The code, tests and documentation were written with the help of Claude Code (Anthropic), an AI coding assistant. The Earth-from-orbit background in the team image and on the demo's title slide is AI-generated and marked as such. All data and figures come from NASA FIRMS, processed by the project's code.
